clinician.trajectory_summary: A 13-year-old boy presented with progressive vision loss and difficulty opening his eyes (bilateral ptosis). Clinical examination revealed restricted eye movements in all gaze directions, exotropia (5°), and best-corrected visual acuity of LogMAR 0.3 bilaterally. Multimodal ocular imaging demonstrated characteristic findings: retinal hyperpigmentation on fundus photography, choroidal thinning (223-224 μm subfoveal thickness), deep retinal capillary density loss on OCTA, ellipsoid band interruption on SD-OCT, and hyperreflective deposits above the retinal pigment epithelium. Superior temporal visual field defects with centripetal reduction were documented on perimetry. Systemic evaluation revealed: (1) prior growth retardation treated with growth hormone therapy, (2) current dizziness and fatigue, (3) cardiac conduction abnormalities on 24-hour Holter monitoring (intermittent first-degree AV block and partial second-degree type I AV block), with unremarkable echocardiography, and (4) brain MRI showing diffuse demyelinating lesions in white matter of cerebral hemispheres, inner capsule, middle cerebral crura, pons, and medulla oblongata. The constellation of progressive ophthalmoplegia, pigmentary retinopathy, cardiac conduction abnormalities, CNS involvement, and systemic manifestations is pathognomonic for Kearns-Sayre Syndrome. The known final diagnosis explicitly states that 'complete evidence obtained from ocular examination and evaluation of other organs as well as from gene detection supported the final diagnosis of KSS.'

Superior temporal visual field defects with centripetal reduction were documented on perimetry. Systemic evaluation revealed: (1) prior growth retardation treated with growth hormone therapy, (2) current dizziness and fatigue, (3) cardiac conduction abnormalities on 24-hour Holter monitoring (intermittent first-degree AV block and partial second-degree type I AV block), with unremarkable echocardiography, and (4) brain MRI showing diffuse demyelinating lesions in white matter of cerebral hemispheres, inner capsule, middle cerebral crura, pons, and medulla oblongata. The constellation of progressive ophthalmoplegia, pigmentary retinopathy, cardiac conduction abnormalities, CNS involvement, and systemic manifestations is pathognomonic for Kearns-Sayre Syndrome. The known final diagnosis explicitly states that 'complete evidence obtained from ocular examination and evaluation of other organs as well as from gene detection supported the final diagnosis of KSS.'
